title: How should you prepare for case interviews if you have six weeks or more?
description: Starting from zero? A simple, realistic plan for 42 days of case interview prep, with what to do each week.
hook: With six weeks or more, spend weeks one and two learning the course, the frameworks and the vocabulary while doing easy cases, weeks three and four doing four or five cases a week plus every drill and every case type, and weeks five and six doing hard cases, practising with friends twice a week and polishing your fit stories. Six weeks is enough to build real skill from zero rather than cramming. The trick is to give each phase a different job: learn, then test, then make it reliable under pressure.
body:
In this guide

  • The plan at a glance
  • Weeks 1 and 2: learn the language and the method
  • Weeks 3 and 4: test yourself on unfamiliar cases
  • Weeks 5 and 6: make it reliable under pressure
  • Check your progress at the end of each phase
  • Focused sprints for any weak skill
  • A sample week in the middle phase
  • Mistakes that waste a long run-up
  • If you fall behind
  • Check yourself

The plan at a glance

WeeksJobCases per weekPartner cases
1 and 2Course, frameworks and glossary; easy cases2 to 3Optional
3 and 4Every drill and every case type4 to 5At least 1 a week
5 and 6Hard cases, fit stories, rest the day before4 to 52 a week

That is roughly 20 to 26 cases over six weeks: enough to see every common case type several times without burning out. If you set your interview date on PrepForCase, your home page shows which phase you are in. If you have more than six weeks, stretch the first phase and keep a lighter rhythm until six weeks out.

Weeks 1 and 2: learn the language and the method

The job of this phase is to build vocabulary and basic mechanics, so that later practice is about judgement rather than not knowing what EBITDA means.

  • The course. Do the eleven lessons of the course, one a day. Take notes in your own words.
  • Frameworks. Learn the 11 core frameworks and, more importantly, why each branch is there.
  • The glossary. Read the consulting glossary and test yourself on ten terms a day. If you are new to business, add how businesses make money.
  • Easy cases. Two or three a week from the casebook, out loud. Clear prompts in familiar industries are fine for now.
  • Daily maths. Ten minutes in the maths drill, every day for the whole six weeks.

Start a list of possible fit stories now, too. Write one line for every experience that might show leadership, teamwork, persuasion, resilience or impact. You will choose from it later.

Weeks 3 and 4: test yourself on unfamiliar cases

The job now is to apply the method to businesses you do not know and to find your real weaknesses.

  • Four or five cases a week, deliberately mixed: profitability, market entry, M&A, private equity, pricing, growth, operations, public sector and market sizing. The case types page lists all seventeen with the first questions to ask.
  • Every drill. Rotate through structure, maths, charts and sizing in the drills so no skill goes untrained.
  • Partner cases. At least one a week with another person. Practising with a partner shows how to run them and give feedback.
  • Fit. Turn your list into six to eight stories using the fit interview guide.

Weeks 5 and 6: make it reliable under pressure

By now you can solve cases. The job of the final phase is to do it consistently, when tired, nervous or thrown a surprise.

  • Hard cases against the clock: ambiguous prompts, dense exhibits, unfamiliar industries, about 30 minutes each.
  • Friends twice a week. Ask them to interrupt, challenge your numbers and add one surprise fact mid-case.
  • Fit stories rehearsed out loud, two a day, with someone asking follow-ups.
  • Full mock interviews. At least two that combine a fit section and a case, in the format you expect.
  • Rest the day before. Read your fixes, rehearse two stories, check logistics and sleep. On the morning, use the 30-minute warm-up.

Check your progress at the end of each phase

Simply adding more cases each week does not guarantee progress. At the end of weeks two, four and six, score one case on the same six dimensions: clarifying the objective, structuring, business judgement, maths accuracy, chart reading and the final recommendation. Use a partner's notes, not only your own rating.

Then let the scores decide the next phase. Suppose at the end of week four your maths is reliable but your recommendations wander. Spend week five's drill time on recorded 60-second closes rather than more sums. If your structures still look the same for every case, add more unusual prompts, such as public sector and operations cases.

Track evidence, not feelings. "Found the driver of the profit drop before brainstorming in three of my last four cases" is progress. "Felt more confident" may be true but tells you nothing about what to do next.

Focused sprints for any weak skill

Weak skillFive-day sprint
Structure and hypothesis30 structures, two minutes each, compared with the model, in the structuring drill
Maths and charts30 chart reads at 90 seconds each in the chart drill, plus ten minutes of speed maths a day
RecommendationTen recorded 60-second closes; count filler words, then re-record answer-first
Clarify and recap20 case openings: recap and three questions only, graded by a partner
Case leadershipFive cases where you announce the next step after every answer; your partner tallies each time you wait
CommunicationDaily voice exercises from the speaking guide plus one recorded full case

A sample week in the middle phase

DayMain sessionDaily extras
MondayCase: profitability, soloMaths drill; review
TuesdayCase: market entry, with a partnerMaths drill; review
WednesdayStructure and chart drills; one fit storyMaths drill
ThursdayCase: M&A, soloMaths drill; review
FridayCase: a market sizing caseMaths drill; review
SaturdayCase: an unfamiliar industry, with a partnerFit story
SundayLight day: read your fixes, restNone

Keep one day lighter every week. Coming back to corrected mistakes after a gap usually teaches more than grinding the same case type in one exhausting session.

Mistakes that waste a long run-up

  • Staying in learning mode too long. If you are still reading in week three and have done only a couple of cases, move on. Cases teach faster than reading.
  • Peaking in week four. Heavy volume early leads to fatigue late. Hold the pace steady and finish strong.
  • Avoiding partners. It is easy to keep practising alone for six weeks. Book partner sessions in advance.
  • Polishing what is already good. Each phase should start from your weakest scores, not your favourite activities.

If you fall behind

You will miss days. Everyone does. Do not double up; pick up where the plan is today. If you lose a whole week, shorten the first phase, not the last: realistic practice and fit preparation in weeks five and six matter most.

Check yourself

1. It is the end of week two and you have read everything but done one case. What do you change?

Show the answer

Move straight into the middle phase: four or five cases next week, starting with familiar case types, plus your daily maths. Your reading will make sense once you use it.

2. Your end-of-phase scores show strong structure, weak chart reading. What does next week's drill time look like?

Show the answer

A chart sprint: six chart reads a day at 90 seconds each for five days, saying the insight and the so-what in one sentence, plus the usual ten minutes of maths. Keep the full cases going.

3. If you do ten minutes of maths every day for 42 days, how many hours is that?

Show the answer

42 × 10 = 420 minutes, which is 7 hours.

Where to go next

Start with lesson 1 today. If you are coming from science, engineering, medicine or law, read preparing without a business background too, and if your timeline shortens, switch to the three-week plan.
outro: Set your interview date on PrepForCase and your home page will show which step of the plan you are on. Next in this topic: Can you prepare for case interviews without a business background?
